title: Vectors & Vector Spaces
summary: Vectors as data, norms, dot product, and linear independence — the foundation every embedding, feature vector, and similarity metric builds on.

slides.markdown:
A **vector** is an ordered list of numbers — and in ML/CS that list is usually a **feature vector** or an **embedding**: a word, image, or user represented as coordinates in space.

Think of a movie as `[action, romance, runtime_hrs]` — every recommender, search index, and embedding model is really vectors plus arithmetic on them.

- A vector is both a **data structure** (array of numbers) and a **geometric object** (point/arrow in space).
- **Vector spaces** give consistent rules for adding and scaling vectors.
- Similarity, dimensionality reduction, and gradients all build on this.

slides.subTitle: Addition and scalar multiplication
slides.markdown:
**Vector addition** combines vectors component-wise: `[2,2] + [3,1] = [5,3]`. Geometrically, place the second vector's tail at the first's head — the sum is the diagonal of the parallelogram they form.

**Scalar multiplication** stretches or shrinks a vector: `2 * [1,2] = [2,4]`, same direction, doubled length. A negative scalar flips its direction.

![Vector addition via the parallelogram rule](assets/vector-addition.svg)

slides.subTitle: Dot product
slides.markdown:
The **dot product** `a·b = Σ aᵢbᵢ` is a single number capturing how much two vectors point the same way.

Algebraically it's multiply-and-sum component-wise. Geometrically, `a·b = |a||b|cos(θ)` — largest when vectors align, zero when perpendicular, negative when opposing.

It's the core ML primitive: a neuron's weighted sum, attention scores, and similarity search are all dot products underneath.

slides.subTitle: Norms: L1, L2, L∞
slides.markdown:
A **norm** measures a vector's "size." Which one you pick changes what "small" means.

| Norm | Formula | Measures | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1 | Σ\|xᵢ\| | total movement (Manhattan) | Lasso regularization, sparse solutions |
| L2 | √(Σxᵢ²) | straight-line (Euclidean) length | most distance/similarity metrics |
| L∞ | max\|xᵢ\| | the single worst coordinate | robustness/error bounds |

Decide by what you're penalizing: L1 to push toward exact zeros, L2 for typical distance, L∞ when one bad coordinate should dominate the score.

slides.subTitle: Cosine similarity vs Euclidean distance
slides.markdown:
**Cosine similarity** measures only the angle between vectors, ignoring magnitude: `cos(θ) = (a·b)/(|a||b|)`. Two vectors pointing the same way score 1, even if one is 100x longer.

**Euclidean distance** measures actual straight-line distance and *does* care about magnitude.

Use cosine similarity when scale shouldn't matter — comparing a short and a long document by topic. Use Euclidean distance when magnitude is meaningful — comparing raw sensor readings or pixel intensities.

slides.subTitle: Linear independence
slides.markdown:
A set of vectors is **linearly independent** if none of them can be written as a combination of the others — no vector is redundant.

Formally: the only way `c1*v1 + c2*v2 + ... = 0` is if every `cᵢ = 0`. If some other combination also hits zero, the set is dependent — one vector adds no new direction.

Why it matters: independent features carry distinct information; near-dependent (collinear) features cause unstable, blown-up coefficients in regression.

slides.subTitle: Basis and dimension
slides.markdown:
A **basis** is a minimal set of linearly independent vectors whose combinations reach every vector in the space. The **dimension** is how many vectors that takes.

In 2D, any two non-parallel vectors form a basis — everything else is `a*v1 + b*v2`. A 300-dimensional embedding space needs 300 independent directions to represent every point.

Changing basis doesn't change the space — it changes the coordinates you use to describe the same points.

slides.subTitle: Orthogonality and orthonormal bases
slides.markdown:
Two vectors are **orthogonal** if their dot product is zero — geometrically, perpendicular. A basis is **orthonormal** if its vectors are mutually orthogonal *and* each has length 1.

Orthonormal bases are the cheapest to compute with: projecting onto one is just a dot product, no matrix inversion needed. PCA and Fourier bases are built orthonormal precisely so you can decompose and reconstruct signals cheaply.

Gram-Schmidt is the standard recipe for turning any basis into an orthonormal one.

slides.subTitle: High-dimensional geometry
slides.markdown:
Your 3D intuition actively misleads you past a few dozen dimensions. In high dimensions:

- Almost all the volume of a hypercube sits near its corners, not its center.
- Random vectors become **nearly orthogonal** to each other by default.
- Pairwise distances **concentrate** — everything looks roughly equidistant, hurting nearest-neighbor search.

This is the **curse of dimensionality**: "nearby points are similar" needs re-checking whenever features scale up, which is exactly why dimensionality reduction (SVD/PCA) matters.
